clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant; heterozygous DNAJB6 variants clustering in the glycine/phenylalanine-rich (G/F) domain act by a dominant-negative mechanism that impairs chaperone anti-aggregation function.
Presents as a myofibrillar myopathy with rimmed vacuoles and aggregates of myotilin, desmin, TDP-43 and DNAJB6 itself.
Usually adult-onset (childhood-onset in some), with proximal and sometimes distal limb weakness.
Cardiac involvement is characteristically mild or absent, unlike many other myofibrillar myopathies.
Creatine kinase ranges from normal to moderately elevated.
Muscle MRI often shows a selective pattern of involvement that aids diagnosis.
Formerly designated LGMD1D (and LGMD1E in older schemes).
Late respiratory muscle involvement is possible and warrants monitoring.
reference.pathophysiology: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy D1 is an autosomal dominant myofibrillar-type dystrophy caused by heterozygous variants in DNAJB6 on chromosome 7q36.3, which encodes a ubiquitously expressed HSP40/DnaJ co-chaperone that partners with HSP70 to prevent the aggregation of misfolded and aggregation-prone proteins. Disease-causing missense changes cluster in the glycine/phenylalanine-rich (G/F) domain and act by a dominant-negative mechanism that cripples the anti-aggregation activity of the chaperone complex, so poly-ubiquitinated and Z-disc proteins accumulate within the myofibre. The result is a myofibrillar myopathy with rimmed vacuoles and aggregates of myotilin, desmin, TDP-43 and DNAJB6 itself, typically presenting in adulthood with proximal and sometimes distal limb weakness. Unlike several other myofibrillar myopathies, cardiac involvement is characteristically absent or mild, although late respiratory muscle weakness can develop.
additionalDifferentials: Other myofibrillar myopathies (myotilin, desmin, filamin C, BAG3, ZASP/LDB3)
additionalInvestigations: Next-generation sequencing gene panel or whole-exome sequencing including DNAJB6
Muscle biopsy (myofibrillar pathology, rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates)
Muscle MRI to define the selective pattern of involvement
Baseline ECG and echocardiography given the differential diagnosis
redFlags: Symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation such as morning headache and unrefreshing sleep
New cardiac symptoms prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Progression is usually slow over decades, and independent ambulation is often preserved into later life. Respiratory monitoring is advised because late respiratory involvement can occur.
pitfalls: Rimmed vacuoles may be misread as sporadic inclusion body myositis, delaying genetic diagnosis.
Dominant inheritance can be missed with de novo variants or marked variable expressivity.
Distal-onset cases may be classified as a distal myopathy.
Assuming prominent cardiac involvement, as in other myofibrillar myopathies, can be misleading.
management: Recognise there is no disease-specific drug therapy and use physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve function, prevent contractures and provide orthoses and mobility aids
Undertake respiratory surveillance with pulmonary function testing, introducing non-invasive ventilation for the late respiratory involvement that can occur
Perform baseline and periodic cardiac assessment, although cardiac involvement is characteristically mild or absent
Deliver multidisciplinary neuromuscular rehabilitation to maintain the ambulation often preserved into later life
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and assess at-risk relatives
Refer to specialist neuromuscular services for confirmation and long-term follow-up
